Elastoplasticity
Available in laboratory
×
Drucker–Prager, nonassociated perfect plasticity

Pressure-dependent yielding with separate controls for frictional strength and plastic volume change.

Drucker–Prager uses a smooth conical yield surface. More compressive mean stress raises the shear stress needed to yield; a separate dilation parameter controls the accompanying plastic volume change.

What it describes
Frictional strength
The shear yield stress depends on confinement.
Nonassociated plastic flow
Strength and dilatancy can be adjusted independently.
Perfect plasticity
The yield surface does not expand with accumulated plastic strain.
Explore the response

Choose Drained triaxial. Compare the response at two confining stresses, starting each run from an admissible initial state. Look for the change in shear stress at yielding.

Keep the friction slope fixed and vary the dilatancy slope to explore the plastic volume response.

Material parameters

Use consistent units and a material-specific parameter set. Laboratory presets illustrate behaviour.

Parameter	Meaning	Example value and units
E · Young modulus	Sets the slope of the elastic axial stress–strain response.	30000000 · Pa
ν · Poisson ratio	Controls the balance of lateral and axial elastic deformation.	0.25 · dimensionless
M · Friction slope	Raises shear yield stress as mean stress increases.	1.2 · dimensionless
M_d · Dilatancy slope	Controls plastic volume change; use source-consistent values between zero and the friction slope.	0.2 · dimensionless
c · Yield intercept	Sets the shear-stress intercept at zero mean stress.	10000 · Pa
Starting state

Supply the initial effective stress and void ratio. A numerically admissible state still needs to represent the material’s actual preparation.

Scope and limitations

The Atlas formulation uses three-dimensional small strain, fixed spatial axes and compression-positive stress and strain. Stresses are effective stresses; the surrounding drainage formulation supplies any pore-pressure response. Changing elapsed time alone does not produce creep or relaxation.

This implementation has constant elasticity, no hardening and no separate tensile cutoff. The yield intercept is defined in p–q space and is not directly a Mohr–Coulomb cohesion.

model-hypoplastic-sand-igs97.js.result.t.profile:
Hypoplasticity
Available in laboratory
×
Sand hypoplasticity with intergranular strain (1997)

Sand hypoplasticity with additional memory of very small strains and changes in loading direction.

The Niemunis–Herle intergranular-strain extension adds a tensor describing recent deformation to the von Wolffersdorff sand law. This lets unloading, reversal and continued loading have different stiffness.

What it describes
Small-strain stiffness
The extra memory changes stiffness over a small deformation scale.
Direction-dependent reloading
Reversing or turning the strain direction changes the response.
Pressure and density effects
The sand host retains its stress- and density-dependent behaviour.
Explore the response

Compare a monotonic path with a small strain cycle. Follow unloading and reloading stiffness, keeping the complete initial stress, density and memory fixed.

Material parameters

The three limiting void ratios share a zero-pressure reference and must retain their dense–critical–loose ordering. Example coefficients are not a calibration for every sand. The additional memory parameters belong to the selected IGS extension.

Parameter	Meaning	Example value and units
φ_c · Critical friction angle	Sets the frictional limit at critical state.	0.5235987755982988 · rad
h_s · Granular hardness	Sets the pressure scale for stiffness and density limits.	5800000000 · Pa
n · Pressure exponent	Controls how density limits and stiffness change with pressure.	0.28 · dimensionless
e_d0 · Dense limiting void ratio	Locates the dense limit at zero pressure.	0.53 · dimensionless
e_c0 · Critical void ratio	Locates the critical-state density at zero pressure.	0.84 · dimensionless
e_i0 · Loose limiting void ratio	Locates the loose limit at zero pressure.	1 · dimensionless
α · Density influence	Controls the influence of density on the nonlinear response.	0.13 · dimensionless
β · Density stiffness influence	Controls how relative density changes stiffness.	1.05 · dimensionless
R · Memory radius	Sets the scale of very small strain over which direction memory changes.	0.0001 · dimensionless
m_R · Reversal stiffness	Sets the stiffness increase after reversing the strain direction.	5 · dimensionless
m_T · Orthogonal stiffness	Sets the stiffness response when the loading direction turns by a right angle.	2 · dimensionless
β_r · Memory mobilisation	Controls how quickly intergranular strain approaches its limiting magnitude.	0.5 · dimensionless
χ · Stiffness transition	Controls the transition between small-strain and continuing-loading stiffness.	6 · dimensionless
Starting state

Supply the initial effective stress and void ratio. A numerically admissible state still needs to represent the material’s actual preparation. Also specify the full intergranular-strain tensor h. Zero history and a mobilized history describe different starting conditions.

Scope and limitations

The Atlas formulation uses three-dimensional small strain, fixed spatial axes and compression-positive stress and strain. Stresses are effective stresses; the surrounding drainage formulation supplies any pore-pressure response. Changing elapsed time alone does not produce creep or relaxation.

This is the 1997 extension paired with the selected von Wolffersdorff host. ISA and generalized intergranular strain are different extensions. Holding a stationary strain path does not erase memory.

Hypoplasticity
Available in laboratory
×
Sand hypoplasticity · von Wolffersdorff (1996)

A sand model whose stiffness, strength and volume response depend on pressure and density.

The von Wolffersdorff hypoplastic law evolves stress directly from the current stress, void ratio and strain direction. It describes nonlinear behaviour without dividing each increment into a separate elastic and plastic part.

What it describes
Pressure-dependent stiffness
The same strain change can produce a different stress change at another pressure.
Density-dependent shearing
Dense and loose states can have different strength and contraction or dilation.
Explore the response

Choose Drained triaxial. Compare two admissible initial void ratios at the same stress and material parameters. Follow both the stress–strain curve and the volume change.

Material parameters

The three limiting void ratios share a zero-pressure reference and must retain their dense–critical–loose ordering. Example coefficients are not a calibration for every sand.

Parameter	Meaning	Example value and units
φ_c · Critical friction angle	Sets the frictional limit at critical state.	0.5235987755982988 · rad
h_s · Granular hardness	Sets the pressure scale for stiffness and density limits.	5800000000 · Pa
n · Pressure exponent	Controls how density limits and stiffness change with pressure.	0.28 · dimensionless
e_d0 · Dense limiting void ratio	Locates the dense limit at zero pressure.	0.53 · dimensionless
e_c0 · Critical void ratio	Locates the critical-state density at zero pressure.	0.84 · dimensionless
e_i0 · Loose limiting void ratio	Locates the loose limit at zero pressure.	1 · dimensionless
α · Density influence	Controls the influence of density on the nonlinear response.	0.13 · dimensionless
β · Density stiffness influence	Controls how relative density changes stiffness.	1.05 · dimensionless
Starting state

Supply the initial effective stress and void ratio. A numerically admissible state still needs to represent the material’s actual preparation.

Scope and limitations

The Atlas formulation uses three-dimensional small strain, fixed spatial axes and compression-positive stress and strain. Stresses are effective stresses; the surrounding drainage formulation supplies any pore-pressure response. Changing elapsed time alone does not produce creep or relaxation.

The basic law has no additional small-strain direction-memory variable. Multiple reversals can show limitations in reloading stiffness. Atlas uses a restricted compressive-stress and density domain and does not transport finite rotations.

model-modified-cam-clay.js.result.txt.profile:
Critical-State Plasticity
Available in laboratory
×
Modified Cam Clay

A clay plasticity model that connects compression history with yielding and permanent deformation.

Modified Cam Clay describes how a clay changes volume and carries shear stress as it is loaded. A changing yield surface separates elastic response from plastic deformation. Its size records the effect of past plastic compression.

What it describes
Pressure-dependent stiffness
The elastic stiffness increases with mean effective stress and depends on the current void ratio.
Yielding and compression history
Loading inside the yield surface is elastic. Reaching the surface can cause permanent deformation and change the size of the surface.
Contraction, dilation and critical state
Plastic shearing can reduce or increase volume, depending on the stress state. At critical state, shearing can continue without further plastic volume change.
Try changing the compression history

Choose Drained triaxial and Monotonic ramp. Start with a radial effective stress of 100 kPa, an axial / radial stress ratio of 1, void ratio 0.7 and preconsolidation pressure of 200 kPa. These give an initial overconsolidation ratio (OCR) of 2: the preconsolidation pressure is twice the initial mean effective stress.

Compare this with a fresh run using preconsolidation pressure 100 kPa (OCR 1), keeping the other inputs the same. Look at when the stress–strain response changes and how the volume response differs. This isolates the effect of the model’s initial yield-surface size; the two states are illustrative rather than reconstructions of prepared specimens.

Material parameters

These dimensionless example values illustrate behaviour. Calibrate them for the material and stress range you want to represent. The compression indices use natural logarithms.

Parameter	Meaning	Example value and units
M · Critical-state slope	Sets the ratio of deviator stress to mean effective stress at critical state (q = M p).	1.2 · dimensionless
λ · Virgin compression index	Controls compression during virgin loading in specific volume versus natural log of mean effective stress.	0.2 · dimensionless
κ · Swelling index	Controls elastic compression and swelling. It must be smaller than λ.	0.04 · dimensionless
ν · Elastic Poisson ratio	Sets the balance of shear and bulk stiffness in the elastic response.	0.25 · dimensionless
Starting state

Supply the initial effective stress, void ratio e (pore volume divided by solid volume) and preconsolidation pressure p_c (the size of the yield surface). For isotropic stress, OCR = p_c / p. The initial stress must lie on or inside the yield surface. These inputs are independent entries in Atlas; it does not infer a consistent specimen preparation history from them.

Scope and limitations

The Atlas formulation uses three-dimensional small strains and effective stress, with compression positive. It is rate independent: changing the elapsed loading time alone does not produce creep or stress relaxation. Pore-pressure evolution needs a surrounding drainage or fluid formulation; the laboratory reconstructs pore-pressure change for its undrained controls.

Use this profile to explore the basic critical-state response of clay. This formulation has isotropic hardening and no evolving fabric anisotropy, structure/bond degradation or dedicated cyclic-memory mechanism. It requires positive mean effective stress and does not cover mean tensile stress or finite rotations.
